# Object-oriented programming in C++ {#sec-ch-cpp-oop}

> *"I made up the term 'object-oriented' … I did not have C++ in mind."* —
> Alan Kay [@kay1997].

```{python}
from cppbook import run, show, sh, write, compile_sources, run_exe, sanitizer_summary
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- define **classes** with data members, member functions, `const` member
  functions and `static` members, and explain `this`;
- write **constructors** (default, parameterised, with member initialiser
  lists) and **destructors**, predict the **order** of construction and
  destruction, and **prove** why the reverse order is the safe one;
- control access with `public`, `protected` and `private`, and know when a
  **friend** function or class is justified;
- use **inheritance**, **override** member functions, and understand **multiple**
  and **virtual** inheritance — **proving** how many copies of a base class an
  object contains;
- obtain **polymorphism** with **virtual functions**, explain how **vtables**
  implement it, and define **abstract classes** with **pure virtual**
  functions;
- avoid **object slicing**, the missing **virtual destructor**, and the shallow
  copies that the **rule of three/five/zero** prevents;
- **overload operators** with their natural meaning, and **prove** that a
  comparator must be a **strict weak order** for `std::sort`, `std::set` and
  `std::map` to work.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
Building object-oriented programs in C++: classes and the special functions
that create and destroy objects, access control and friendship, derived classes
(with one or several bases, and shared bases), redefining and overriding
functions, polymorphism through virtual and abstract functions, and giving
operators a meaning for new types.
:::

## Intuition: the same blueprints, a stricter builder

The ideas of object-oriented programming — **abstraction**, **encapsulation**,
**inheritance**, **polymorphism** — are the ones of @sec-ch-oop, and they come
from the same place: Simula 67, which Stroustrup used before designing C++
[@dahl1968; @stroustrup1994]. What changes is the builder. Python decides
almost everything **at run time**: an object is a dictionary of attributes,
any method may be added or replaced, every call is looked up by name. C++
decides as much as possible **at compile time**: the members of a class and
their layout are fixed, access is checked by the compiler, an ordinary member
call is a direct jump to known code, and only functions declared `virtual` are
looked up at run time — through a table, in constant time.

The result is the C++ deal again (@sec-ch-c-vs-cpp): more rules to learn, more
errors caught before running, objects as compact as C structures, and you pay
for dynamic dispatch only where you ask for it.

## Classes and objects {#sec-cpp-classes}

A **class** declares data members (the state) and member functions (the
behaviour). Here is a first version of the customer class of the project:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

class Customer {
public:
    Customer(std::uint32_t id, std::string name, std::string surname)   // constructor
        : id_(id), name_(std::move(name)), surname_(std::move(surname)) {}

    std::uint32_t id() const { return id_; }                 // const: does not modify *this
    const std::string& surname() const { return surname_; }
    std::string full_name() const { return name_ + ' ' + surname_; }
    void rename(const std::string& name, const std::string& surname) {
        name_ = name;
        surname_ = surname;
    }

private:
    std::uint32_t id_;
    std::string name_;
    std::string surname_;
};

int main() {
    Customer c(1, "Ada", "Lovelace");
    const Customer& view = c;                    // a read-only view of c
    std::cout << view.id() << ": " << view.full_name() << '\n';
    c.rename("Augusta Ada", "King");
    std::cout << view.full_name() << '\n';       // view sees the change: it is the same object
    // view.rename("x", "y");                    // error: rename is not const
}
""", name="customer.cpp")
```

Things to notice:

- **Member functions** are declared inside the class; short ones are defined
  there too. Inside a member function, the members of the current object are
  used by name (`name_`), and `this` is a pointer to the object itself — the
  `self` of Python, implicit.
- A member function marked **`const`** promises not to modify the object; only
  `const` member functions can be called through a `const` reference or
  pointer. Marking every non-modifying function `const` ("const correctness")
  lets the compiler enforce read-only views.
- The trailing underscore in `id_` is a common naming convention for private
  data members; it is not a language rule.

### `static` members

A `static` data member belongs to the **class**, not to each object — like a
Python class attribute (@sec-classes). A typical use is a counter shared by all
instances:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>

class Ticket {
public:
    Ticket() : number_(++issued_) {}
    int number() const { return number_; }
    static int issued() { return issued_; }      // static member function: no 'this'
private:
    int number_;
    inline static int issued_ = 0;               // one variable for the whole class (C++17 'inline')
};

int main() {
    Ticket a, b, c;
    std::cout << a.number() << b.number() << c.number() << ", issued: " << Ticket::issued() << '\n';
}
""", name="static_member.cpp")
```

## Constructors and destructors {#sec-ctors}

### Constructors

A **constructor** has the name of the class and no return type; it runs when an
object is created and must leave it in a valid state (its invariant holds,
@sec-encapsulation). A class may have several, distinguished by their
parameters (overloading, @sec-overloading):

- the **default constructor** takes no arguments; the compiler generates one
  if you declare no constructor at all;
- **parameterised constructors** take the values needed to build the object;
- the **member initialiser list** (`: id_(id), name_(…)`) initialises members
  *before* the body runs. Use it: members are constructed exactly once, and
  `const` members, references and members without a default constructor
  *can only* be initialised there.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>

class Date {
public:
    Date() : Date(1970, 1, 1) {}                          // default: delegates to the other constructor
    Date(int y, int m, int d) : y_(y), m_(m), d_(d) {
        if (m < 1 || m > 12 || d < 1 || d > days_in_month(y, m))
            throw std::invalid_argument("invalid date");  // never build an invalid Date
    }
    std::string str() const {
        char buf[11];
        std::snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "%04d-%02d-%02d", y_, m_, d_);
        return buf;
    }
    static int days_in_month(int y, int m) {
        static const int days[] = {31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31};
        bool leap = (y % 4 == 0 && y % 100 != 0) || y % 400 == 0;     // Gregorian rule
        return m == 2 && leap ? 29 : days[m - 1];
    }
private:
    int y_, m_, d_;
};

int main() {
    Date epoch, d(2028, 2, 29);
    std::cout << epoch.str() << ' ' << d.str() << '\n';
    try { Date bad(2026, 2, 29); }
    catch (const std::invalid_argument& e) { std::cout << "2026-02-29: " << e.what() << '\n'; }
}
""", name="date.cpp")
```

A constructor that cannot establish the invariant **throws**: then the object
never exists, and no code can ever see an invalid `Date`. (The leap-year rule
is the one of @prp-leap-equivalence.) A constructor with one parameter can be
used by the compiler for **implicit conversions** (`Premium p = 500;`); mark it
`explicit` to forbid that, as in @sec-encapsulation-cpp.

### Destructors and the order of destruction

The **destructor** `~ClassName()` runs when the object's lifetime ends: at the
end of the enclosing block for local objects, at `delete` for heap objects,
when the owning object is destroyed for members. It releases whatever the
object acquired — the RAII principle (@sec-raii). The order is fixed by the
language:

- **construction**: base classes first, then data members in **declaration
  order**, then the constructor body;
- **destruction**: the exact **reverse** — destructor body, members in reverse
  order, then bases; and local objects of a block are destroyed in the reverse
  of the order in which they were created.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

struct Noisy {
    std::string name;
    explicit Noisy(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) { std::cout << "  + " << name << '\n'; }
    ~Noisy() { std::cout << "  - " << name << '\n'; }
};

struct Logger : Noisy {                              // inherits from Noisy (next section)
    Noisy file{"log file"};                          // a member
    Noisy buffer{"buffer"};                          // declared after file
    Logger() : Noisy("logger base") { std::cout << "  (Logger body)\n"; }
};

int main() {
    std::cout << "enter block\n";
    {
        Noisy first("first local");
        Logger log;
        Noisy last("last local");
    }
    std::cout << "left block\n";
}
""", name="order.cpp")
```

::: {#prp-reverse-destruction}
## Why the reverse order is safe
Number objects $1, 2, \dots, n$ in order of construction, and suppose each
object may use (refer to) only objects constructed **before** it. If objects
are destroyed in reverse order $n, n-1, \dots, 1$, then whenever an object is
destroyed, every object it may use is still alive.
:::

*In one line:* last in, first out — an object is torn down while everything it
was built on still stands.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-reverse-destruction
When object $j$ is destroyed, the objects already destroyed are exactly
$n, n-1, \dots, j+1$, i.e. those with numbers greater than $j$. The objects $j$
may use have numbers $i < j$, none of which is among them: all are alive.
Any other order destroys some $i$ before some $j > i$ while $j$ is still alive;
if $j$ uses $i$ (in its destructor, say), it would touch a dead object. So the
reverse order is the only one that is safe for *every* such dependency
pattern. $\blacksquare$
:::

In the output, `last local` is destroyed first; inside `log`, the members go
in reverse declaration order (`buffer` before `log file`), then the base. The
assumption "use only what was built before you" is exactly what the
construction order guarantees for members and bases — a member's initialiser
can use earlier members and the bases, never later ones.

## Access control and friends {#sec-access}

| Specifier | Accessible from | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `public` | everywhere | the interface: what users of the class may call |
| `protected` | the class, its friends and **derived classes** | hooks for subclasses |
| `private` | the class and its friends only | the representation and its invariant |

: Access specifiers {#tbl-access}

Access is checked by the compiler and applies to **classes**, not objects: a
member function can access the private members of *another* object of the
same class (useful in comparisons and copies).

A **friend** is a function or class, declared inside a class with the keyword
`friend`, that gets access to its private members although it is not a member.
Friendship is granted by the class, not taken; it is not inherited and not
transitive. The classic legitimate use is a pair of tightly coupled pieces of
code that belong together but cannot be member functions — such as the output
operator `<<`, whose left operand is a stream, not our object:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>

class Money {
public:
    explicit Money(long long cents) : cents_(cents) {}
    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Money& m);   // a friend function
    friend class Ledger;                                                  // a friend class
private:
    long long cents_;
};

std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Money& m) {             // may read m.cents_
    return os << m.cents_ / 100 << '.' << (m.cents_ % 100 < 10 ? "0" : "") << m.cents_ % 100 << " EUR";
}

class Ledger {
public:
    static void apply_fee(Money& m, long long fee) { m.cents_ -= fee; }  // may modify private data
};

int main() {
    Money m(48000);
    Ledger::apply_fee(m, 250);
    std::cout << m << '\n';
}
""", name="friends.cpp")
```

Every friend weakens encapsulation: the invariant is now the responsibility of
the class **and** its friends. Use friends for operators and for a "partner"
class that is part of the same abstraction (an iterator for its container, a
builder for its product); do not use them as a shortcut around a missing public
function.

## Inheritance {#sec-cpp-inheritance}

### Deriving and overriding

A class can **derive** from a base class, inheriting its members and adding or
redefining some (@sec-inheritance). In C++ the base is listed after a colon,
with an access specifier — almost always `public`, which means "is-a": a
`Contract` *is an* `Interaction`, and can be used wherever an `Interaction` is
expected.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

class Interaction {
public:
    Interaction(int customer_id, std::string date) : customer_id_(customer_id), date_(std::move(date)) {}
    std::string summary() const { return date_ + " customer #" + std::to_string(customer_id_); }
protected:
    int customer_id_;                      // visible in derived classes
    std::string date_;
};

class Appointment : public Interaction {
public:
    Appointment(int customer_id, std::string date, std::string agent)
        : Interaction(customer_id, std::move(date)), agent_(std::move(agent)) {}   // base constructor first
    std::string summary() const {          // redefines (hides) Interaction::summary
        return Interaction::summary() + " with " + agent_;                         // call the base version
    }
private:
    std::string agent_;
};

int main() {
    Appointment a(7, "2026-11-20", "M. Bianchi");
    std::cout << a.summary() << '\n';
    const Interaction& base = a;           // an Appointment IS an Interaction
    std::cout << base.summary() << '\n';   // but which summary is called?
}
""", name="inherit.cpp")
```

The last line calls `Interaction::summary`, not `Appointment::summary`: the
function is chosen from the **static type** of the expression
(`const Interaction&`), at compile time. This is *redefinition*, not
polymorphism. To have the call depend on the actual object, the function must
be **virtual** (@sec-virtual).

### Multiple inheritance

A C++ class may have several base classes. Unlike Python, C++ does not compute
a method resolution order (@sec-mro): if two bases provide the same name, an
unqualified use is **ambiguous** and does not compile; you disambiguate by
naming the base.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>

struct Printable { void describe() const { std::cout << "printable\n"; } };
struct Storable  { void describe() const { std::cout << "storable\n"; } };

struct Report : Printable, Storable {};      // two bases (struct: public by default)

int main() {
    Report r;
    r.Printable::describe();                 // explicit: fine
    r.Storable::describe();
    r.describe();                            // which one? -> ambiguous
}
""", name="multiple.cpp", expect_error=True)
```

### The diamond and virtual inheritance {#sec-virtual-inheritance}

When two bases share a common base, the object would contain the common base
**twice**:

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-cap: "The diamond: Account derives from Customer and from Agent, which both derive from Person. Without virtual inheritance an Account contains two Person subobjects."
flowchart BT
    C["Customer"] --> P["Person"]
    A["Agent"] --> P
    AC["Account (customer who is also an agent)"] --> C
    AC --> A
```

::: {#prp-subobjects}
## How many copies of a base?
In a hierarchy that uses only ordinary (non-virtual) inheritance, an object of
class $D$ contains exactly one subobject of a base class $A$ **for each
distinct path** from $D$ to $A$ in the inheritance graph. With **virtual**
inheritance on every path into $A$, it contains exactly one.
:::

*In one line:* each path of "derives from" arrows embeds its own copy, unless
the base is declared virtual, which makes all paths share one.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-subobjects
Without virtual bases, an object of $D$ is laid out as one subobject for each
*direct* base $B$, followed by $D$'s own members; each $B$ subobject is, in
turn, a complete layout of $B$. Let $N(D, A)$ be the number of $A$
subobjects in a $D$ object and $P(D, A)$ the number of paths from $D$ to $A$.
For $D = A$ both are 1 (the empty path; the object is itself). For $D \ne A$
with direct bases $B_1, \dots, B_k$:
$N(D, A) = \sum_i N(B_i, A)$, because the $A$ subobjects of $D$ are exactly
those inside its direct-base subobjects; and
$P(D, A) = \sum_i P(B_i, A)$, because every path from $D$ starts with an edge
to one $B_i$. The inheritance graph is acyclic (a class cannot derive from
itself), so induction along it (@thm-toposort) gives $N = P$ everywhere. With
virtual inheritance the standard requires that all virtual occurrences of $A$
denote a single shared subobject [@iso14882, §class.mi], so $N = 1$.
$\blacksquare$
:::

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

struct Person { std::string name = "?"; };

struct Customer1 : Person {};
struct Agent1    : Person {};
struct Account1  : Customer1, Agent1 {};            // two Person subobjects

struct Customer2 : virtual Person {};               // virtual inheritance
struct Agent2    : virtual Person {};
struct Account2  : Customer2, Agent2 {};            // one shared Person

int main() {
    Account1 a1;
    a1.Customer1::name = "as customer";
    a1.Agent1::name = "as agent";                    // a different string!
    std::cout << "non-virtual: " << a1.Customer1::name << " / " << a1.Agent1::name << '\n';
    // a1.name = "x";                               // error: ambiguous (two names)

    Account2 a2;
    a2.name = "Ada";                                 // unambiguous: one Person
    std::cout << "virtual: " << a2.Customer2::name << " / " << a2.Agent2::name << '\n';
    std::cout << "sizeof(Account1) = " << sizeof(Account1)
              << ", sizeof(Account2) = " << sizeof(Account2) << '\n';
}
""", name="diamond.cpp")
```

`Account1` holds two `std::string`s (32 bytes each with GCC); `Account2` holds
one, plus two hidden pointers (8 bytes each) that its `Customer2` and `Agent2`
parts use to find the shared `Person`. With virtual inheritance the shared `Person` is reached through an extra
indirection (a pointer or offset stored in the object), and the most derived
class becomes responsible for constructing it. Multiple inheritance of classes
with state is rarely the best design; the common, safe use is inheriting from
several **interfaces** — abstract classes without data (@sec-abstract) — which
is also what Java and C# allow.

## Polymorphism and virtual functions {#sec-virtual}

### Virtual functions

A member function declared **`virtual`** in a base class is chosen at run time
from the **dynamic type** of the object — the type it was created with —
whenever it is called through a pointer or reference to the base. A derived
class **overrides** it by declaring a function with the same signature; the
keyword `override` (C++11) asks the compiler to check that it really overrides
something.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class Interaction {
public:
    explicit Interaction(std::string date) : date_(std::move(date)) {}
    virtual ~Interaction() = default;                       // see "virtual destructors" below
    virtual std::string kind() const { return "interaction"; }
    std::string describe() const { return date_ + " " + kind(); }   // non-virtual, but calls a virtual
protected:
    std::string date_;
};

class Appointment : public Interaction {
public:
    using Interaction::Interaction;                         // inherit the constructor
    std::string kind() const override { return "appointment"; }
};

class Contract : public Interaction {
public:
    using Interaction::Interaction;
    std::string kind() const override { return "contract"; }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Interaction>> history;      // a polymorphic collection
    history.push_back(std::make_unique<Appointment>("2026-11-20"));
    history.push_back(std::make_unique<Contract>("2026-11-27"));
    history.push_back(std::make_unique<Interaction>("2026-12-01"));
    for (const auto& item : history)
        std::cout << item->describe() << '\n';              // dynamic dispatch on kind()
}
""", name="virtual.cpp")
```

One loop treats appointments and contracts **uniformly**; each object answers
`kind()` in its own way. This is **subtype** (or inclusion) **polymorphism**,
the third kind in Cardelli and Wegner's classification after ad hoc
(overloading) and parametric (templates) [@cardelli1985]. It is what lets the
CRM list, search and save "interactions" without knowing in advance how many
kinds there are. For the design to be sound, every override must honour the
base class's contract — the Liskov substitution principle of @sec-lsp.

### How it works: vtables {#sec-vtables .deep}

C++ implementations realise virtual calls with a **virtual table** [@lippman1996;
@itaniumabi]. For each class with virtual functions the compiler builds one
table of function addresses, one slot per virtual function; each object
contains a hidden pointer to its class's table (the **vptr**), set by the
constructor. A call `p->kind()` becomes: load the vptr from `*p`, load the
address in the slot of `kind`, call it — three steps, whatever the size of
the hierarchy. The price is one pointer per object and an indirect call that
the processor cannot inline:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>

struct Plain   { int x; void f() {} };
struct Virtual { int x; virtual void f() {} virtual ~Virtual() = default; };

int main() {
    std::cout << "sizeof(Plain) = " << sizeof(Plain) << ", sizeof(Virtual) = " << sizeof(Virtual) << '\n';
}
""", name="vptr.cpp")
show(r"""
struct Shape { virtual double area() const = 0; virtual ~Shape() = default; };
double total_area(const Shape& s) { return s.area(); }      // one virtual call
""", name="call.cpp")
sh("g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -S call.cpp -o - | sed -n '/^_Z10total_areaRK5Shape:/,/\\.cfi_endproc/p' | "
   "grep -Ev '\\.cfi|endbr'")
```

`Virtual` grows from 4 to 16 bytes: an 8-byte vptr plus `x`, padded to a
multiple of 8 (@prp-padding). The function body is the whole mechanism: load
the vptr from the object (`movq (%rdi), %rax`) and jump to the address stored
in the first slot of the table (`jmp *(%rax)`). When the compiler can prove the
dynamic type — for example for a `final` class or a local object — it
**devirtualises** the call into a direct one.

### Object slicing and virtual destructors

Polymorphism works through **pointers and references**. Copying a derived
object into a base-class *value* **slices** it: only the base part is copied,
and the copy is a genuine base object.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

struct Interaction { virtual ~Interaction() = default; virtual std::string kind() const { return "interaction"; } };
struct Contract : Interaction { std::string kind() const override { return "contract"; } };

void by_value(Interaction i)          { std::cout << "by value:     " << i.kind() << '\n'; }
void by_reference(const Interaction& i) { std::cout << "by reference: " << i.kind() << '\n'; }

int main() {
    Contract c;
    by_value(c);         // sliced: the copy is an Interaction
    by_reference(c);     // polymorphic
}
""", name="slicing.cpp")
```

The second trap concerns destruction. If a derived object is deleted through
a pointer to a base whose destructor is **not** virtual, only the base
destructor runs — undefined behaviour that in practice leaks the derived part:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

struct Base    { ~Base() { std::cout << "~Base\n"; } };                 // NOT virtual
struct Derived : Base {
    std::string data = std::string(100, 'x');                          // owns heap memory
    ~Derived() { std::cout << "~Derived\n"; }
};

int main() {
    Base* p = new Derived;
    delete p;                       // only ~Base runs
}
""", name="nonvirtual_dtor.cpp")
```

**Rule:** a class meant to be used as a polymorphic base must have a
**public virtual destructor** (or a protected non-virtual one, if deletion
through the base must be forbidden) [@cppcoreguidelines, C.35]. GCC warns with
`-Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor` when it can see the problem, and AddressSanitizer
reports it as a `new-delete-type-mismatch`.

### Abstract classes and pure virtual functions {#sec-abstract}

Often the base class has no sensible implementation of a function: what is the
"kind" or the "file format" of a generic interaction? A **pure virtual**
function, declared with `= 0`, has no implementation in the base and **must**
be overridden; a class with at least one pure virtual function is **abstract**
and cannot be instantiated. An abstract class with only pure virtual functions
and no data is an **interface** — the C++ counterpart of Python's abstract base
classes (@sec-inheritance).

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class Interaction {                                         // abstract base
public:
    virtual ~Interaction() = default;
    virtual std::string kind() const = 0;                   // pure virtual
    virtual std::string details() const = 0;
    virtual bool matches(const std::string& text) const {   // virtual with a default
        return details().find(text) != std::string::npos;
    }
};

class Appointment : public Interaction {
public:
    Appointment(std::string when, std::string agent) : when_(std::move(when)), agent_(std::move(agent)) {}
    std::string kind() const override { return "appointment"; }
    std::string details() const override { return when_ + ", agent " + agent_; }
private:
    std::string when_, agent_;
};

class Contract : public Interaction {
public:
    Contract(std::string number, long long premium_cents) : number_(std::move(number)), premium_(premium_cents) {}
    std::string kind() const override { return "contract"; }
    std::string details() const override {
        return "policy " + number_ + ", premium " + std::to_string(premium_ / 100) + " EUR";
    }
private:
    std::string number_;
    long long premium_;
};

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Interaction>> v;
    v.push_back(std::make_unique<Appointment>("2026-11-20 10:00", "M. Bianchi"));
    v.push_back(std::make_unique<Contract>("CAR-0042", 48000));
    for (const auto& i : v)
        std::cout << i->kind() << ": " << i->details()
                  << (i->matches("Bianchi") ? "   <- matches 'Bianchi'" : "") << '\n';
    // Interaction i;   // error: cannot declare a variable of abstract type
}
""", name="abstract.cpp")
```

This is, in miniature, the design of the CRM's interactions (@sec-crm-design).

## Copying objects: the rule of three, five and zero {#sec-rule-of-three}

When an object is copied (`Customer b = a;`, pass by value, return by value,
`push_back` into a vector), C++ calls its **copy constructor**; when it is
assigned (`b = a;`), its **copy assignment operator**. If you do not write
them, the compiler generates versions that copy each member. That is right for
members that manage themselves (`int`, `std::string`, `std::vector`), and
**wrong** for a class that owns a raw resource: two objects end up owning the
same memory, and both destructors free it.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <cstring>

class Buffer {                                   // owns a raw array: needs care
public:
    explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : size_(n), data_(new char[n]) { std::memset(data_, 0, n); }
    ~Buffer() { delete[] data_; }
    // no copy constructor / copy assignment written: the compiler copies the POINTER
private:
    std::size_t size_;
    char* data_;
};

int main() {
    Buffer a(16);
    Buffer b = a;                                // b.data_ == a.data_
}                                                // ~b frees the array, then ~a frees it again
""", name="double_free.cpp", sanitize="address", flags=("-O0",), filter_lines=sanitizer_summary)
```

Hence the classic **rule of three**, a piece of C++ folklore from the early
1990s popularised by Meyers [@meyers2005]: if a class needs a user-written destructor, copy constructor or
copy assignment, it almost certainly needs all three. C++11 added **move**
operations (transfer ownership instead of copying, as `std::unique_ptr` does,
@sec-raii), making it the **rule of five**. The modern advice is the **rule of
zero** [@cppcoreguidelines, C.20]: design classes so that they need **none**
of the five — let members that already manage their resources
(`std::string`, `std::vector`, `std::unique_ptr`) do the work. The CRM's
classes follow the rule of zero: none of them declares a destructor or a copy
operation, except the virtual destructor of the abstract base.

## Operator overloading {#sec-operator-overloading}

C++ lets a class define the meaning of most operators for its objects:
`a + b` becomes a call `operator+(a, b)` (or `a.operator+(b)`). This is what
makes `std::string`'s `+` and `==`, and `std::cout << x`, possible. Overloaded
operators should **behave like the built-in ones** (`+` should not subtract,
`==` should be an equivalence): readers rely on the usual laws.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <compare>
#include <iostream>
#include <set>
#include <string>

class Money {
public:
    explicit Money(long long cents = 0) : cents_(cents) {}
    Money& operator+=(Money other) { cents_ += other.cents_; return *this; }
    friend Money operator+(Money a, Money b) { return a += b; }          // defined via +=
    friend Money operator*(Money a, int k) { return Money(a.cents_ * k); }
    friend auto operator<=>(const Money&, const Money&) = default;     // C++20: <, <=, >, >=, ==, !=
    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, Money m) {
        return os << m.cents_ / 100 << '.' << (m.cents_ % 100 < 10 ? "0" : "") << m.cents_ % 100;
    }
private:
    long long cents_;
};

int main() {
    Money premium(21050), fee(250);
    Money total = premium + fee * 2;
    std::cout << "total: " << total << " EUR\n";
    std::cout << std::boolalpha << (premium < total) << ' ' << (premium == Money(21050)) << '\n';
    std::set<Money> distinct{Money(500), Money(100), Money(500)};       // uses operator<
    std::cout << distinct.size() << " distinct amounts, smallest " << *distinct.begin() << '\n';
}
""", name="operators.cpp")
```

C++20's defaulted `operator<=>` ("spaceship") compares the members in
declaration order — lexicographically, which is a strict total order whenever
the members' orders are (@thm-lex-order) — and generates all six comparison
operators.

### What a comparator must satisfy {#sec-strict-weak}

`std::sort`, `std::set` and `std::map` accept a custom "less than". The CRM,
for instance, sorts customers by surname **ignoring case**, so that `rossi`
and `Rossi` come together. Such a comparator does not distinguish all distinct
values (`"rossi" != "Rossi"`), so it is not a strict total order; the standard
requires only a weaker property [@iso14882, §alg.sorting]:

::: {#def-strict-weak}
## Strict weak order
A relation $\prec$ on a set $S$ is a **strict weak order** if it is
irreflexive (never $a \prec a$), transitive, and **incomparability is
transitive**: writing $a \sim b$ when neither $a \prec b$ nor $b \prec a$,
$a \sim b$ and $b \sim c$ imply $a \sim c$.
:::

::: {#thm-strict-weak}
## A strict weak order is a total order of equivalence classes
If $\prec$ is a strict weak order on $S$, then $\sim$ is an equivalence
relation (@def-equivalence), and $\prec$ is well defined on the equivalence
classes, where it is a strict total order. Sorting with $\prec$ therefore
groups equivalent elements together and orders the groups.
:::

*In one line:* "neither is smaller" behaves like "equal", so the comparator
sorts *groups* of equivalent elements as a total order would.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-strict-weak
*$\sim$ is an equivalence.* Reflexive: $a \prec a$ is false, so $a \sim a$.
Symmetric: the definition of $a \sim b$ is symmetric in $a$ and $b$.
Transitive: this is the third axiom.

*Well defined on classes.* Suppose $a \prec b$, $a \sim a'$ and $b \sim b'$; we
show $a' \prec b'$. First, $a' \prec b$: otherwise either $b \prec a'$, and
then $a \prec b \prec a'$ gives $a \prec a'$ by transitivity, contradicting
$a \sim a'$; or $b \sim a'$, and then $a \sim a'$ and $a' \sim b$ give
$a \sim b$, contradicting $a \prec b$. By the symmetric argument on the right,
$a' \prec b$ and $b \sim b'$ give $a' \prec b'$.

*Total on classes.* For two different classes $[a] \ne [b]$ we have
$a \not\sim b$, i.e. $a \prec b$ or $b \prec a$; irreflexivity and
transitivity carry over from $\prec$. $\blacksquare$
:::

Comparing `tolower(surname)` strings, for example, is a strict weak order: it
is the strict total order of strings applied to a *key*, and any comparator of
the form "compare $k(a) < k(b)$" for a key function $k$ is a strict weak order
whose classes are the elements with equal keys. A comparator that breaks the
axioms is **undefined behaviour** for the standard algorithms — `std::sort` may
produce garbage or read outside the range. The commonest mistake is using
`<=`, which is not irreflexive. The debug mode of GCC's library
(`-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG`) checks the axioms on the elements it compares:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v{5, 3, 5, 1, 5, 2};
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a <= b; });   // NOT a strict weak order
    for (int x : v) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}
""", name="bad_comparator.cpp", flags=("-O0", "-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG"),
    filter_lines=lambda l: "Error:" in l)
```

## Designing class hierarchies {#sec-cpp-design}

The design principles of @sec-solid apply unchanged; C++ adds a few concrete
rules that follow from this chapter [@cppcoreguidelines, section C]:

| Situation | C++ rule |
|---|---|
| a type with an invariant | `class` with private data; constructors establish the invariant, `const` member functions read it |
| plain data with no invariant | `struct` with public members |
| a family of types used uniformly | an abstract base class with pure virtual functions and a public virtual destructor; derived classes `override` |
| several "abilities" | inherit from several interfaces (abstract classes without data); avoid multiple inheritance of state |
| "has-a" relationship | a data member (composition, @sec-composition), not inheritance |
| owning a polymorphic object | `std::unique_ptr<Base>`; containers of `std::unique_ptr<Base>` |
| resources | rule of zero; RAII members |

: Class design rules in C++ {#tbl-cpp-design}

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** The CRM's object model (@sec-crm-design, requirement R9 of
@sec-crm-brief) is this chapter applied: an abstract class `Interaction` with a
public virtual destructor and pure virtual functions (`kind`, `details`, and
`add_fields`, which `to_record` calls when saving), a virtual `matches` with a
default implementation for searching, and two concrete classes `Appointment`
and `Contract` that `override` them. A `Customer` **owns** its
interactions in a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Interaction>>`, so they are
listed, searched and saved polymorphically, and destroyed automatically when
the customer is deleted (rule of zero, R5). `Customer` keeps its data private
behind `const` accessors and a validating `update`; dates compare with a
defaulted `operator<=>`; and the listing sorts customers with a case-insensitive
comparator — a strict weak order, as @thm-strict-weak requires.
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Forgetting `virtual`**: the base version is called through base pointers
  (redefinition is not overriding). Write `override` on every override, and
  the compiler will catch mismatched signatures.
- **No virtual destructor** in a polymorphic base: derived destructors are
  skipped.
- **Object slicing**: passing or storing polymorphic objects by value. Use
  references, pointers, or `std::unique_ptr`.
- **Calling virtual functions from constructors or destructors**: during
  construction the object is still of the base type, so the base version runs.
- **Rule of three violations**: a raw owning pointer member with the default
  copy operations → double free. Prefer the rule of zero.
- **Initialiser list order**: members are initialised in *declaration* order,
  not in the order of the list (GCC warns with `-Wreorder`).
- **Comparators that are not strict weak orders** (`<=`, inconsistent keys):
  undefined behaviour in `std::sort`, `std::set`, `std::map`.
- **Overloaded operators with surprising meaning**, or `==` without the
  matching `!=` and `<` (C++20 `<=>` and `= default` avoid this).
- **Friends as a shortcut** around encapsulation.
:::

## Summary

- A class bundles private data with public member functions; `const` member
  functions promise not to modify; `static` members belong to the class.
- Constructors (default, parameterised, delegating, with initialiser lists)
  establish the invariant or throw; destructors release resources. Destruction
  runs in the **reverse** order of construction, the only order safe for every
  dependency (@prp-reverse-destruction).
- `public`/`protected`/`private` are checked at compile time; **friends** get
  private access, granted by the class.
- Inheritance (`: public Base`) models "is-a". Without `virtual`, functions are
  chosen by the static type. Multiple inheritance is resolved by explicit
  qualification; an object holds one base subobject per inheritance path, or
  one in total with **virtual inheritance** (@prp-subobjects).
- **Virtual functions** give run-time polymorphism through **vtables** (one
  pointer per object, constant-time dispatch); **pure virtual** functions make
  **abstract classes**. Polymorphic bases need **virtual destructors**; beware
  **slicing**.
- Rule of three/five, and better the **rule of zero**.
- **Operator overloading** should respect the usual laws; comparators must be
  **strict weak orders** (@thm-strict-weak).

## Exercises

::: {#exr-cpp7-order}
Predict the output of
```cpp
struct A { A() { std::cout << "A"; } ~A() { std::cout << "a"; } };
struct B { B() { std::cout << "B"; } ~B() { std::cout << "b"; } };
struct C : A { B b1, b2; C() { std::cout << "C"; } ~C() { std::cout << "c"; } };
int main() { C c; }
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Construction: base `A`, then members `b1`, `b2` in declaration order, then the
body: `ABBC`. Destruction in reverse: body of `~C`, members `b2`, `b1`, then
base: `cbba`. Output: `ABBCcbba`.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp7-paths}
Classes: `A`; `B : A`; `C : A`; `D : B, C`; `E : D, A`. How many `A`
subobjects does an `E` contain? Which declarations would you make `virtual` to
have exactly one?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Paths from `E` to `A`: E→D→B→A, E→D→C→A, E→A: three, so three `A` subobjects
(@prp-subobjects). (GCC also warns that the direct base `A` of `E` is
inaccessible due to ambiguity.) To have one, every path must enter `A`
virtually: `B : virtual A`, `C : virtual A`, `E : D, virtual A`.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp7-comparator}
Which of these are strict weak orders on strings? (a) `a.size() < b.size()`;
(b) `a.size() <= b.size()`; (c) `a < b || a.size() < b.size()`;
(d) `tolower_string(a) < tolower_string(b)`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) Yes: a key comparison with key = length; classes = strings of equal
length. (b) No: `a <= a` is true, violating irreflexivity. (c) No: take
`a = "b"`, `b = "aa"`: `a < b` is false but `a.size() < b.size()` is true, so
`a ≺ b`; and `b < a` (`"aa" < "b"`) is true, so `b ≺ a` as well — both
directions hold, which contradicts irreflexivity via transitivity
($a \prec b \prec a$ gives $a \prec a$). (d) Yes: a key comparison with key =
lower-case version (@thm-strict-weak).
:::

::: {#exr-cpp7-shapes}
Write an abstract class `Policy` with pure virtual functions
`long long annual_premium_cents() const` and `std::string product() const`,
and two concrete classes `CarPolicy` (premium = base + 10% per accident in the
last five years) and `HomePolicy` (premium proportional to the insured value).
Store some policies in a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Policy>>` and print the
total premium. Where is the virtual destructor needed, and why?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```cpp
class Policy {
public:
    virtual ~Policy() = default;                 // needed: unique_ptr<Policy> deletes through the base
    virtual long long annual_premium_cents() const = 0;
    virtual std::string product() const = 0;
};
class CarPolicy : public Policy {
public:
    CarPolicy(long long base, int accidents) : base_(base), accidents_(accidents) {}
    long long annual_premium_cents() const override { return base_ + base_ * 10 * accidents_ / 100; }
    std::string product() const override { return "car"; }
private:
    long long base_; int accidents_;
};
class HomePolicy : public Policy {
public:
    explicit HomePolicy(long long insured_cents) : insured_(insured_cents) {}
    long long annual_premium_cents() const override { return insured_ / 1000; }   // 0.1%
    std::string product() const override { return "home"; }
private:
    long long insured_;
};
// std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Policy>> v; v.push_back(std::make_unique<CarPolicy>(50000, 2)); ...
// long long total = 0; for (const auto& p : v) total += p->annual_premium_cents();
```
The virtual destructor is needed in `Policy`, because each `std::unique_ptr<Policy>`
deletes a `CarPolicy` or `HomePolicy` through a `Policy*`.
:::
